outline:
This is a history course of western classical music, of which the definition, according to The New Harvard Dictionary of Music and The Oxford Dictionary, is "art music” or "serious music", that written in a Western musical tradition, using an established form. "Classical music is generally considered to be serious and to have a lasting value.”
The styles of various periods will be introduced, from the Medieval, Renaissance, Classical, Romantic, to the Contemporary eras. The goal of this course is helping students to equip a general comprehension of Classical Music in terms of basic elements of musical art, technical theory, historical, social and cultural background extends to related arts and humanities.
In addition, basic elements of music notation reading and theory will also be made known to the students.
Other genres such as Alternative Rock and related fields will be interlaced with the Classical Music.

In order to pursue the most accurate references and info, the major key-points and terminology used in this course will be in English or original European text.
(There are requirements to fulfill this course such as Midterm & Final Exams, as well as in-class presentation or performance. If you're not interested in serious music genre, please DO NOT take this course.)
schedule:
1st week: Introduction to Western Art Music—Greek origin as the foremost culture before Christianity entered Europe

2nd week: The Medieval Period--folk music, church music in relation to arts and culture

3rd week: From Medieval to Renaissance period--Madrigals, church music, dance music.

4th week: Renaissance period--from Monophony to Polyphony; Introduction to Italian composers, artists, and some of the most popular musical instruments; the Reformed Church and Martin Luther that not only changed the society and belief system but also aethesticism in arts.

5th week: Baroque--Louis XIV and his influence on French music,in comparison to English Baroque

6th week: Baroque--Italian and French legends--Corelli, Lully and Couperin, Introduction to Concerto Grosso

7th week: Baroque--Italian and French legends continues--Vivaldi, Scarlatti, and Rameau--Court Dance and French Ballet

8th week: Baroque--Comparison among Handel, Telemann, and J.S.Bach

9th week: Baroque--J.S. Bach in-depth--his string works, orchestral music, choral music, keyboard music, and Fugues.

10th week: Midterm Exam

11th week: Classical period (Classicism)--The Age of Enlightenment--Frederick the Great as a passionate patron of music and art; Danish royal house contributing Jean-Jacques Rousseau's ideology in Denmark; Catherine the Great and The Hermitage **Students' presentations begin**

12th week: The First Viennese School; Gluck and Habsburg family; Marie Antoinette

13th week: Romantic period--Beethoven and the beginning of Romantic era; how Schubert was influenced by Beethoven

14th week: The pinnacle of Romantic era--Chopin, Schumann, Brahms, Liszt, Tchaikovsky, to the late Romantic period

15th week: A counterpart of Romantic style with Naionalism--Music by Bohemian and Russian composers; 19th Century Russian ballet and music

16th week: Impressionist Music, The Second Viennese School and related art styles in the period. The Contemporary Music--from Twelve- tone music (The 2nd Viennese School) to Existentialism, music of Minimalism, and experimental music; comparison with other genres

18th week: Final Exam

flexible_learning.content: A list of repertoire will be given for the students to listening to. Students are required to give answers according to the music played during the exams. It is also mandatory for students to do an in-class presentation. They may find partners within the class or present alone. Topics can be various genres and styles as long as it’s musical art related. Musical instruments' performance or singing can also be one of the formats for the presentation.
